followUps:
Already-running Pods keep working, but new Pods may start without a fresh certificate. The data plane keeps its last configuration, so existing traffic flows.

A new sidecar or ztunnel needs istiod to get its certificate and config. With injection, the injector webhook lives in istiod too, so with a fail-open webhook the Pod starts without a sidecar (a security gap), and with fail-closed it is not created. Run istiod with 2 or more replicas and a PodDisruptionBudget so this is rare.

Skip a mesh when you have few services, a single team, or no need for mTLS, traffic shifting or uniform telemetry.

A mesh adds CPU and memory, extra hops (a little added latency per proxy hop), upgrade work and a new thing to debug. With 5 services, a library or an ingress controller plus NetworkPolicies is often enough. It pays off when dozens of services in several languages need the same identity, policy and metrics without changing code.

HBONE is HTTP-Based Overlay Network Encapsulation, the tunnel ambient mode uses between ztunnels.

It wraps ordinary TCP streams in an HTTP/2 CONNECT request carried over an mTLS connection (port 15008). Many application connections share one tunnel between two nodes, and the certificate identities of the workloads are used for authentication. The result is mTLS without touching the application Pod and without a sidecar.

Put a waypoint only where a service needs layer-7 features; everything else stays on cheap L4 ztunnel.

Needs that justify one: HTTP routing or canary weights, retries and timeouts, L7 AuthorizationPolicy (methods, paths, JWT claims), and HTTP metrics. Start with one waypoint per namespace; give a hot or sensitive service its own so it scales alone. If a namespace only needs mTLS and "service A may call B", use no waypoint at all.

Balance per request, not per connection. gRPC uses one long-lived HTTP/2 connection, so connection-level balancing sends all calls to one version.

The mesh proxy (Envoy) understands HTTP/2 and gRPC, so a VirtualService with weights 95/5 splits each call separately. Without a proxy in the path, a client-side connection pool sees one connection and the split can be 100/0 or 0/100. Check the result with per-version request metrics, not by counting Pods.

Use expand and contract so v1 and v2 both work with the database at every moment.

  1. Expand: add the new column or table (backwards compatible); v1 ignores it.
  2. Deploy v2 that writes both old and new shapes; canary 5% to 100%.
  3. Backfill old data.
  4. Contract later: remove the old column once v1 is gone.

Never ship a destructive migration in the same release as the canary, or rollback breaks.

code.title: Retry amplification across layers
code.python:
# Retry amplification: every layer retries when the layer below fails
TRIES = 4      # 1 first try + 3 retries
LAYERS = 3     # edge -> service A -> service B -> database

def main():
    calls = 1  # calls arriving at the current layer per user request
    print("each layer makes", TRIES, "attempts when the next hop fails")
    for layer in range(1, LAYERS + 1):
        print("layer", layer, "receives", calls, "call(s)")
        calls *= TRIES  # every call below is multiplied by the attempts
    print("database receives", calls, "call(s)")
    # Retrying at one layer only keeps the multiplier at TRIES
    print("retry at one layer only: database receives", TRIES)

main()

followUps:
It stops Envoy from ejecting every unhealthy host: if too many hosts are unhealthy, it sends traffic to all of them anyway.

The default panic threshold is 50%. If fewer than 50% of hosts in a cluster are healthy, Envoy ignores health status and balances across all hosts. For example, 6 of 10 hosts failing means all 10 receive traffic, because sending everything to the 4 survivors would overload and kill them too. It trades some errors for avoiding a total outage.

Only retry safe or idempotent requests; a POST is usually not safe unless it carries an idempotency key.

Safe cases: the request never reached the server (connection refused, reset before sending, Istio's connect-failure and refused-stream). A 503 from an overloaded upstream may have been processed, so retrying a plain POST can charge a card twice. With an Idempotency-Key header the server deduplicates, and retrying 502/503/504 becomes fine.

IPs are temporary and shared; identity should follow the workload, not the address.

Pods get a new IP at every restart or reschedule, with autoscaling you might have 40 IPs in a day, and NAT, node-level SNAT or a shared egress can hide the real source. A rule such as "allow 10.1.4.7" then allows whatever runs there next. A certificate bound to a service account stays correct and is cryptographically proven, so the policy reads "cart may call payments".

Move in steps, watching for plain-text callers before you block them.

  1. Install the mesh with PERMISSIVE (accepts both).
  2. Inject or enrol all workloads; check telemetry for connections where the security policy is not mutual_tls.
  3. Fix or exempt the stragglers (jobs, legacy, health probes).
  4. Switch one namespace to STRICT, watch error rates, then repeat.
  5. Set mesh-wide STRICT last.

Keep the rollback to PERMISSIVE ready.

code.title: AuthorizationPolicy evaluation order

followUps:
It is denied: with mTLS not in use, the request has no authenticated principal, so a rule that requires a principal cannot match.

If the workload has an ALLOW policy listing principals, a plain-text caller has an empty principal and falls through to the default deny (HTTP 403 or a reset connection at L4). That is why STRICT mTLS must be on first; in PERMISSIVE mode, a policy that only names principals blocks every plain-text client, which is a good way to find them, but also an outage if unplanned.

AUDIT logs what a policy would match without changing the decision, so you can test rules in production safely.

Add an AUDIT policy copying the planned rule, then look at the logs or telemetry for 1 to 2 weeks. If the log shows only expected callers, convert it to ALLOW/DENY. It needs an audit-capable provider configured, and it is supported in a limited way (for example, in ambient mode check the current docs for your version).

Because anyone who can create a Pod in a namespace can run code with that namespace's service accounts and secrets.

A Pod can mount any Secret or ConfigMap in its namespace, use any ServiceAccount there (its token can have more rights than the creator), and with a permissive security context mount the host filesystem or run privileged and take over the node. So "create pods" is effectively "read all secrets and maybe become root on the node". Pair it with Pod Security admission to limit this.

They are special verbs that let someone raise their own power, so grant them almost never.

  • escalate: create or edit a Role with permissions you do not hold yourself.
  • bind: create a binding to a Role even if you lack its permissions.
  • impersonate: act as another user, group or service account (--as), for example cluster-admin.

Without these, the API server blocks you from granting more than you have.

The enforce-version label pins which release of the standards applies, so a cluster upgrade does not suddenly block existing workloads.

Without it, latest is used and newer Kubernetes versions can add stricter checks. For example pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version: v1.30 keeps the rules from 1.30. Pin it, then bump the version deliberately after testing with warn and audit set to the newer version.

Ephemeral containers are checked by Pod Security admission just like normal containers.

The debug container is added to a running Pod, and its securityContext must satisfy the namespace level; in a restricted namespace, kubectl debug with a default (root) image is rejected. Pass a profile such as --profile=restricted or set the user and capabilities explicitly. Some teams keep a separate debug namespace policy and grant the ephemeralcontainers permission only to on-call staff.

Make the webhook fail open for non-critical namespaces, run it highly available, and exclude the system namespaces.

  • 3 replicas spread over zones, a PodDisruptionBudget, and resource requests.
  • Exclude kube-system and the policy engine's own namespace so it can always start.
  • Set a short timeoutSeconds (3 to 5) and choose failurePolicy: Ignore where a miss is tolerable, Fail only for high-risk rules.
  • Prefer ValidatingAdmissionPolicy for simple checks, since it needs no webhook.

Write test cases as YAML fixtures with the expected result and run them on every policy change.

Kyverno has kyverno test and Gatekeeper has gator test; both take policy plus sample resources and assert pass or fail. Keep 2 cases per rule: one that must be blocked, one that must pass. Then apply the policies in audit mode to a staging cluster and check the reports before enforcing.

code.title: NetworkPolicy isolation model
code.python:
# NetworkPolicy ingress model: a pod selected by any policy is isolated,
# and only sources listed by a policy may reach it. Others stay open.
policies = {"api": ["web"], "db": ["api"]}   # target -> allowed sources

def allowed(src, dst):
    if dst not in policies:        # not selected by any policy: open
        return True
    return src in policies[dst]    # isolated: only listed sources

tests = [("web", "api"), ("web", "db"), ("api", "db"), ("db", "web"), ("db", "api")]
for src, dst in tests:
    print(src + " -> " + dst + ": " + ("allow" if allowed(src, dst) else "deny"))

followUps:
Cilium and Calico add layer-7 rules, deny rules, FQDN rules and cluster-wide policy, which the core API lacks.

Core NetworkPolicy is allow-only, per namespace, and speaks only IPs, labels and ports. Cilium or Calico add explicit deny, ordering/priority, global (cluster-scoped) policies, DNS name egress (api.example.com), HTTP method and path rules, and richer logging. They are CNI-specific, so using them ties you to that CNI.

NetworkPolicy blocks at the network level (L3/L4); AuthorizationPolicy decides by identity and request details (L7). Use both for defence in depth.

NetworkPolicy works even for pods outside the mesh and stops any traffic that bypasses a sidecar. AuthorizationPolicy knows who the caller is (SPIFFE ID) and what it asks for (method, path), which IP rules cannot. If one layer is misconfigured, the other still limits the damage.

The issuer only says which identity provider signed the certificate, and many unrelated people can get a valid one from the same issuer.

With keyless signing, the public issuer (for example GitHub Actions OIDC) issues certificates to every repository. If you check only the issuer, any project's workflow could sign an image that you would accept. You must also match the subject, such as the exact repository, workflow file and branch, e.g. repo:myorg/shop/.github/workflows/release.yml@refs/heads/main.

Mirror them into your own registry, scan them, and either verify the vendor's signature or re-sign them with your key.

Steps: pull a pinned version by digest, scan it, verify the upstream signature if there is one, push to your registry, sign with your identity. The admission policy then needs only one rule ("signed by us"). Add a policy exception list for the few images you cannot mirror, and update on a schedule so security patches arrive.

Namespace isolation is not enough when tenants are untrusted, need a different kernel-level boundary, or need their own cluster-wide resources.

All pods share one kernel, so a container escape reaches the node and its neighbours. Use separate clusters for regulated data (PCI) or hostile code, and sandboxed runtimes (gVisor, Kata) when you run customer-supplied code on shared nodes at the cost of 10 to 30 percent CPU or slower startup. Teams that need CRDs, custom admission or different Kubernetes versions also need their own cluster (or virtual clusters).

Give teams guardrails they cannot edit, plus self-service inside them.

  • Platform owns policies (Kyverno/VAP, PSA labels, quotas) in a separate repo and namespace; teams only get edit in theirs.
  • Teams request namespaces through a pull request or portal; the pipeline creates them with defaults.
  • Policies cannot be removed by tenants because RBAC excludes policy kinds and namespace labels.
  • Exceptions are time-limited objects reviewed by the platform team.

Weigh the failure behaviour and where the secret lives: ESO copies the value into a Kubernetes Secret, the CSI driver mounts it straight into the Pod.

ESO: works with env vars and any workload, easy to use, but the value is stored in etcd (so encrypt it) and the sync can lag. CSI driver: no Secret object unless you ask for one, fresh at mount time, but each Pod calls the store at startup (rate limits, startup dependency) and needs the driver on every node. I pick ESO for simplicity, CSI for strict no-etcd needs.

KMS v2 uses one data key for many secrets instead of calling the KMS for each one.

The API server creates a data encryption key (DEK), encrypts the secrets locally with it, and has the KMS encrypt only the DEK. v1 made a KMS call per secret, so listing 5,000 secrets meant thousands of calls. v2 caches the DEK, rotates it when the KMS key changes, and keeps the cluster fast and able to start when the KMS is briefly slow.
